full_prose_under_review.title: Collaborative Drug Therapy Management in a Retail Drug Store: Patients, Referral and Consent, Disease States, Controlled Substances and Vaccines
full_prose_under_review.topic: Collaborative practice / Retail drug business setting
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: The retail drug business limb of M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c)(5) and its restatement in 247 CMR 16.03(5) and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e): the 18-year age floor, the extension of current therapy, the named disease states and co-morbidities, the disease-state reference, referral, notice and consent sentences, the community pharmacy written referral, consent and record formalities in 247 CMR 16.03(5)(c)-(d), 16.04(1)(a)-(b) and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)3.-5., the Health Facility registration exemption in § 24B1/2(d), the Schedule II through V bar, the statutory conditions on Schedule VI prescriptions, vaccine administration under the agreement, and M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B3/4 on regulations defined and limited by the statute
learning_objectives: State which patients and disease states a retail collaborative practice agreement may reach, including the 18-year age floor and the requirement that the agreement specifically reference each co-managed disease state.
Compare the statute and 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)1. on extending current therapy, the dosage actions allowed and the co-morbidities reached, and identify the course safe on either reading.
Apply the Schedule II through V bar and the statutory conditions on Schedule VI prescriptions to a retail fact pattern.
Apply the community pharmacy referral, consent and record formalities, including the 24-hour consent copy and the consent-form statement required by 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)4.
Explain vaccine administration under a community pharmacy agreement and the setting requirements that still apply to it.

orientation.text: M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c) lists the settings in which collaborative drug therapy management is allowed, and clause (5) is the one for the retail drug store. It allows the practice by a collaborating pharmacist in a retail drug business, as registered in section 38 of chapter 112 and limited by this section, with supervision by a physician according to the terms of his collaborative practice agreement, and limited to the following: patients 18 years of age or older; an extension by 30 days of current drug therapy prescribed by the supervising physician; and administration of vaccines or the modification of dosages of medications prescribed by the supervising physician for asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, congestive heart failure, HIV or AIDS, osteoporosis and co-morbidities identified by the supervising physician for the individual patient along with the primary diagnosis. The words limited to the following make the list a ceiling rather than a set of examples. The clause was inserted by St. 2008, c. 528, § 3, An Act establishing collaborative drug therapy management, approved January 15, 2009, and the current text of clause (5), including the age floor and the 30-day extension, reads as it was enacted.

The same clause adds three sentences that decide which patients and which conditions a particular agreement actually reaches. The collaborative practice agreement shall specifically reference each disease state being co-managed, so a condition that appears in the statutory list is not co-managed for anyone until the agreement names it. A patient shall be referred by a supervising physician to that physician's collaborating pharmacist, which ties the referral to the physician's own collaborator rather than to any pharmacist who holds an agreement with someone. And the patient shall be given notice of the collaboration and shall consent to the collaboration, two requirements rather than one. Put together, a retail patient is a person 18 years of age or older, referred by the supervising physician to that physician's collaborating pharmacist, notified and consenting, for a disease state the agreement specifically references. What a referral is, what the definition of patient adds, and who qualifies to collaborate at all are taught in the section on the foundations of collaborative practice; the written referral, consent and record formalities that the regulations attach to the community pharmacy agreement are taken up below.

The Board of Registration in Pharmacy restates the setting in 247 CMR 16.03(5), and the Board of Registration in Medicine does the same in 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e). 247 CMR 16.03 allows the practice by pharmacists meeting the requirements of 247 CMR 16.02(1) and authorized by a supervising physician pursuant to a current collaborative practice agreement, and 247 CMR 16.03(5) names Community Pharmacies (retail drug business settings) licensed by the Board pursuant to M.G.L. c. 112, § 39, subject to the restrictions listed and pursuant to a current agreement that includes the requirements that follow. Community pharmacy and retail drug business describe the same setting. The first requirement, 247 CMR 16.03(5)(a), is Patient Age: patients must be 18 years of age or older, which matches the statute. The age item is stated for the setting as a whole, so it applies to every patient under a community pharmacy agreement and not only to a patient for whom the pharmacist prescribes.

The regulations turn the statute's referral, notice and consent sentence into paperwork, and most of it is written as something the agreement must provide that the supervising physician will do. Under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(c), in accordance with 243 CMR 2.12, the collaborative practice agreement must provide that the supervising physician will provide a written referral of the patient to the authorized pharmacist; specify the primary diagnosis for the patient and any secondary diagnoses in the written referral or a subsequent referral; provide a copy of the written referral of the patient to the authorized pharmacist for CDTM services to the patient; and obtain the patient's written informed consent to the collaboration in the collaborative practice agreement and provide a copy of the consent to the patient. 247 CMR 16.04(1) makes the same two documents part of the agreement itself: in the community pharmacy setting the CDTM agreement shall include a written referral of a specific patient from the supervising physician to an authorized pharmacist, and the written consent of the patient to the CDTM agreement. 243 CMR 2.12(1) says the same in the Board of Registration in Medicine's definition of the agreement, and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)3. repeats the four referral and consent items. The medicine regulation adds one requirement the pharmacy regulation does not state: under 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)4., the patient's written consent form shall include the words "The pharmacist shall not replace the physician as the principal medical decision maker." A consent form lacking that sentence falls short of 243 CMR 2.12 even though nothing in 247 CMR 16.03(5) asks for it.

Keeping the records is split between the two professionals in a way that is easy to blur. Under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(d), headed Record of Referral and Consent, the authorized pharmacist and supervising physician must maintain a written record of both the individual patient referral and the patient's written informed consent to the collaboration in the patient's records which are maintained by the authorized pharmacist and the supervising physician, so each of them keeps a record of both documents. The same paragraph, in accordance with 243 CMR 2.12, then gives the supervising physician three duties of his own: maintain the original patient consent to the referral in the record in the custody of the supervising physician; transmit a copy of the patient's consent to the authorized pharmacist within 24 hours; and provide copies of the referral and consent to the patient in a timely manner. 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)5. states the same record duties. The 24 hours belong to the physician's transmission of the consent copy to the pharmacist; the copies owed to the patient carry no hour count, only the words in a timely manner. The separate duty in 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)2. concerning copies of prescriptions, modifications and discontinuations is taught in the section on prescribing under a collaborative practice agreement.

One more subsection of the statute is addressed to the store rather than to the pharmacist. Under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(d), a retail drug business practicing in collaborative drug therapy management under this section shall not be required to register as a Health Facility under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(2)(d). That is the statute's own cross-reference; in the current 105 CMR 700.004, paragraph (A)(2)(d) is Nurse Midwife in the list of practitioners, and Health Facility registration appears at 105 CMR 700.004(A)(3)(d). The subsection speaks to the business and to that registration only. It says nothing about the pharmacist's own registration: the Department registration a collaborating pharmacist holds for the purpose of prescribing is a separate requirement, taught in the section on prescribing under a collaborative practice agreement.

The regulations then describe what the pharmacist may do in terms that are not the statute's. Under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)1., and in the same words under 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)6., an authorized pharmacist currently registered by the Department to prescribe and possess controlled substances, who practices in a community pharmacy pursuant to an agreement that includes individually developed prescriptive practice guidelines under which the supervising physician has authorized the pharmacist to prescribe, may do two things. First, extend current drug therapy by 30 days for not more than two 30 day periods, or as may otherwise be specifically authorized by the supervising physician in the referral of the patient and as provided in the agreement. Second, initiate, modify or discontinue dosages of medications prescribed by the supervising physician for the same eight conditions the statute names, and for co-morbidities listed among those eight and identified by the supervising physician along with the primary diagnosis in the referral. Set beside clause (5), three differences stand out. The statute speaks of an extension by 30 days; the regulations allow up to two 30-day periods, or more where the referral and the agreement specifically provide. The statute speaks of the modification of dosages; the regulations add initiating and discontinuing. And the statute reaches co-morbidities identified by the supervising physician for the individual patient, while the regulations confine co-morbidities to conditions among the eight.

Neither regulation says that its wider words displace the statute, and the statute does not say in terms what becomes of a regulation worded more widely than it. What M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B3/4 does say is that the boards' rules and regulations shall govern each collaborative practice agreement and shall be defined and limited by section 24B1/2, chapter 94C and other applicable statutes. That sentence points toward the statute as the outer limit, but whether the second 30-day period or the initiating power in the regulations goes beyond that limit is a question of reading that no text resolves. The course that is safe on either reading is to stay within the narrower wording on each point: one extension of 30 days of current therapy prescribed by the supervising physician; dosage changes to medications the supervising physician prescribed for a listed condition the agreement specifically references; co-morbidities only where the condition is among the eight and the supervising physician identified it along with the primary diagnosis in the referral; and a new prescription only where the statutory conditions on initial Schedule VI prescriptions, taken up below, are met. The co-morbidity point runs the other way from the other two, because there the regulation is the narrower text, and a pharmacist acting under both regulations is bound by it.

Controlled substances are dealt with from two directions. The statute addresses the document: no collaborative practice agreement in the retail drug business setting may permit the prescribing of schedule II through V controlled substances, as defined in section 3 of chapter 94C. The regulations address the pharmacist: under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)3. and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)7., no authorized pharmacist in a community pharmacy may prescribe or be authorized to prescribe Schedule II through V controlled substances. The range runs through Schedule V, so a Schedule V product is inside the bar, and an agreement term that purports to authorize such prescribing confers nothing, whatever the supervising physician intends and however closely the drug relates to a listed condition. Schedule VI is the category the clause leaves open, and the Department's regulation states the same ceiling for a collaborating pharmacist practising in a retail setting, who may issue a prescription for a controlled substance in Schedule VI only; that provision, with the registration and other prescribing requirements around it, is taught in the section on prescribing under a collaborative practice agreement.

The Schedule VI prescription a retail pharmacist may issue is hedged by three statutory conditions, and each can fail on its own. Under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c)(5), a pharmacist in the retail setting who has a collaborative practice agreement with a supervising physician which specifically allows initial prescriptions for referred patients of the supervising physician may issue prescriptions for schedule VI controlled substances, as defined in clause 6 of section 3 of chapter 94C. The agreement must specifically allow initial prescriptions; an agreement that allows collaborative management in general does not. Such prescriptions shall be for a patient diagnosis specified in the supervising physician's individual referral of that patient, so a diagnosis the pharmacist forms, or one the patient reports, is not enough. And a copy of the prescription shall be sent to the supervising physician within 24 hours. 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)4. and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)8. put the same authority as something the supervising physician may confer, for the diagnoses specified in the supervising physician's patient referral. The regulations' separate copy duty in 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)2. is taught in the section on collaborative prescribing, and what the Schedule VI category contains is taught in the section on Schedule VI.

Vaccines are where the statute and the regulations are arranged most differently. Clause (5) places the administration of vaccines in the same phrase as the modification of dosages of medications prescribed by the supervising physician for the eight named conditions, and its words do not state separately whether that list of conditions reaches the vaccine limb. 247 CMR 16.03(5)(b) states vaccine administration as an item of its own: pharmacists, as authorized pursuant to a collaborative practice agreement, may administer vaccines; 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)2. says the same. No disease list is attached to that item, and the authority it describes is the one the agreement confers, so a pharmacist whose agreement does not authorize vaccine administration has none under this paragraph. The age item in 247 CMR 16.03(5)(a) and the referral, notice and consent requirements of the statute apply to a vaccine patient as to any other. On every reading the agreement must authorize vaccine administration, and the patient must be a referred, notified and consenting patient 18 years of age or older. Beyond that the readings part. If the statute's list of conditions reaches the vaccine limb, it reaches it only through the words prescribed by the supervising physician for, so on that reading the vaccine must be one the supervising physician prescribed for one of the eight named conditions, or for a co-morbidity identified by the supervising physician for the individual patient along with the primary diagnosis. The regulations' vaccine item asks only that the administration be authorized pursuant to the agreement, and those words do not supply a prescription by the supervising physician. The course that meets the narrowest reading of clause (5), and the regulations as well, therefore has all of these parts: the agreement authorizes vaccine administration; the agreement specifically references the disease state; the patient is a referred, notified and consenting patient 18 years of age or older; and the supervising physician prescribed the vaccine for that named condition or identified co-morbidity. A vaccine given on the agreement's general authorization without that prescription, or a vaccine unrelated to a named condition or identified co-morbidity, is within the regulations' separate vaccine item, but it rests on the regulations' reading, which the statute may not support: M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B3/4 provides that the boards' rules and regulations shall be defined and limited by section 24B1/2, and no text settles which reading is right. Pharmacist administration that rests on authority other than a collaborative practice agreement is taught in the section on pharmacist administration, and pharmacist prescribing of hormonal contraception is taught in its own section.

worked_examples.scenario: A supervising physician signs a written referral of a 63-year-old patient with congestive heart failure to his collaborating pharmacist at a community pharmacy and has the patient sign a consent to the collaboration. The consent form says nothing about who makes medical decisions, and the physician sends the pharmacist a copy of the consent three days later.
steps: 247 CMR 16.03(5)(c) requires the agreement to provide that the supervising physician will give a written referral, specify the primary and any secondary diagnoses, and obtain the patient's written informed consent and give the patient a copy.

243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)4. requires the patient's written consent form to include the statement that the pharmacist shall not replace the physician as the principal medical decision maker, and this form lacks it.

247 CMR 16.03(5)(d) and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)5. require the supervising physician to keep the original consent in his own record and transmit a copy of the consent to the authorized pharmacist within 24 hours; three days misses that period.
worked_examples.resolution: Two formalities have failed: the consent form lacks the statement 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)4. requires, and the consent copy reached the pharmacist after 24 hours. The error invited is checking the paperwork against 247 CMR 16.03(5) alone and treating a signed referral and consent as enough.

worked_examples.scenario: A supervising physician refers a 52-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes to her collaborating pharmacist at a community pharmacy. The agreement references diabetes, and the referral names diabetes as the primary diagnosis and major depressive disorder as a co-morbidity. The pharmacist proposes to adjust the dose of the antidepressant the physician prescribed.
steps: Check the setting limits first: the patient is 18 or older, referred by the supervising physician to that physician's collaborating pharmacist, and the agreement references diabetes, a listed condition.

Under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c)(5) the dosage power reaches co-morbidities identified by the supervising physician for the individual patient along with the primary diagnosis, which on its words could include depression.
Under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)1.b. and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)6.b. the co-morbidities reached are those listed among the eight named conditions, and major depressive disorder is not among them.
Section 24B3/4 makes the regulations govern each agreement, and a pharmacist bound by both regulations is bound by their narrower wording here.
worked_examples.resolution: The antidepressant dose change is outside what the regulations allow and should be returned to the supervising physician. The error the facts invite is reading the co-morbidity words off the statute alone and missing that the regulations confine co-morbidities to the eight listed conditions.

worked_examples.scenario: A collaborative practice agreement for a retail pharmacy covers hyperlipidemia and hypertension. The supervising physician adds a clause authorizing the pharmacist to prescribe a Schedule IV sleep aid for referred patients who report insomnia, and signs a note approving each such prescription in advance.
steps: Identify the schedule: the product is in Schedule IV, which lies inside the range Schedule II through V.
Apply the statute: no collaborative practice agreement in the retail drug business setting may permit the prescribing of schedule II through V controlled substances, so the clause authorizes nothing.

Apply the regulations: no authorized pharmacist in a community pharmacy may prescribe or be authorized to prescribe Schedule II through V controlled substances, so the advance approval does not help either.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacist may not prescribe the sleep aid under the agreement. The trap is treating the physician's written approval, or an agreement clause, as capable of reaching a Schedule II through V substance when both the statute and the regulations close that door.

worked_examples.scenario: A referred 40-year-old patient with hypertension, notified and consenting, asks her retail collaborating pharmacist for an initial Schedule VI prescription for a new antihypertensive. The agreement allows the pharmacist to modify dosages and extend therapy for hypertension but says nothing about initial prescriptions.
steps: The diagnosis condition is met: hypertension is specified in the supervising physician's individual referral and referenced in the agreement.
The agreement condition is not met: the statute allows Schedule VI prescriptions only where the agreement specifically allows initial prescriptions for referred patients of the supervising physician.
Extension and modification powers do not supply that condition, because the statute makes the specific allowance of initial prescriptions a separate requirement.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacist should not issue the initial prescription and should refer the request to the supervising physician. The error invited is assuming that authority to modify or extend therapy for a referred diagnosis carries authority to start a new prescription.

worked_examples.scenario: A community pharmacist's agreement authorizes vaccine administration for referred patients. A supervising physician refers a consenting 17-year-old with asthma for an influenza vaccine, and the pharmacist reasons that the vaccine item in the regulations carries no disease or age wording of its own.
steps: 247 CMR 16.03(5)(b) allows pharmacists, as authorized pursuant to a collaborative practice agreement, to administer vaccines, with no disease list attached.
247 CMR 16.03(5)(a) is a separate requirement for every community pharmacy agreement: patients must be 18 years of age or older, and the statute says the same.
The absence of age words in the vaccine item does not lift the age floor stated for the setting.
worked_examples.resolution: The patient cannot be vaccinated under the collaborative practice agreement because she is under 18. The trap is reading the vaccine item on its own and forgetting that the age requirement governs every patient in the retail setting.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What minimum patient age applies to collaborative drug therapy management in a retail drug business?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Patients 18 years of age or older, under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c)(5), 247 CMR 16.03(5)(a) and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)1.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which conditions does the statutory retail limb name for the modification of dosages?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, congestive heart failure, HIV or AIDS, and osteoporosis, together with co-morbidities identified by the supervising physician for the individual patient along with the primary diagnosis.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must a retail collaborative practice agreement say about the disease states being co-managed?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It shall specifically reference each disease state being co-managed.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How do the statute and 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)1.a. differ on extending current drug therapy?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The statute speaks of an extension by 30 days of current therapy prescribed by the supervising physician; the regulation allows extension by 30 days for not more than two 30 day periods, or as otherwise specifically authorized by the supervising physician in the referral and as provided in the agreement.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which co-morbidities may a community pharmacist manage under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)1.b.?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Co-morbidities listed among the eight named conditions and identified by the supervising physician along with the primary diagnosis in the referral.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B3/4 say about the relationship between the collaborative practice regulations and the statute?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The rules and regulations shall govern each collaborative practice agreement and shall be defined and limited by section 24B1/2, chapter 94C and other applicable statutes.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which controlled substance schedules are closed to a retail collaborative practice agreement?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Schedules II through V: no agreement in the retail drug business setting may permit their prescribing, and no community pharmacist may prescribe or be authorized to prescribe them.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What three statutory conditions attach to a Schedule VI prescription issued by a retail collaborating pharmacist?
retrieval_prompts.answer: An agreement that specifically allows initial prescriptions for referred patients of the supervising physician; a patient diagnosis specified in the supervising physician's individual referral of that patient; and a copy of the prescription sent to the supervising physician within 24 hours.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 247 CMR 16.03(5)(b) provide about vaccines in a community pharmacy?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Pharmacists, as authorized pursuant to a collaborative practice agreement, may administer vaccines.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must a community pharmacy collaborative practice agreement provide that the supervising physician will do about referral and consent?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Provide a written referral of the patient to the authorized pharmacist; specify the primary diagnosis and any secondary diagnoses in the written referral or a subsequent referral; provide a copy of the written referral to the authorized pharmacist; and obtain the patient's written informed consent to the collaboration and provide a copy of the consent to the patient.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Within what time must the supervising physician transmit a copy of the patient's consent to the authorized pharmacist in a community pharmacy?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Within 24 hours, under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(d) and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)5.; the original consent stays in the record in the supervising physician's custody.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What statement must the patient's written consent form include under 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)4.?
retrieval_prompts.answer: "The pharmacist shall not replace the physician as the principal medical decision maker."

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Must a retail drug business practicing collaborative drug therapy management register as a Health Facility?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(d) provides that it shall not be required to register as a Health Facility under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(2)(d), a cross-reference the current regulation places at 105 CMR 700.004(A)(3)(d).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which session law inserted the retail limb of M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: St. 2008, c. 528, § 3, approved January 15, 2009; the current text of clause (5) reads as enacted.

quick_review.text: M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c)(5) allows collaborative practice by a collaborating pharmacist in a retail drug business, with supervision by a physician according to the terms of the agreement, limited to the items the clause lists.
Retail patients must be 18 years of age or older under the statute, 247 CMR 16.03(5)(a) and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)1.
The statute allows an extension by 30 days of current drug therapy prescribed by the supervising physician.

The statute allows administration of vaccines or the modification of dosages of medications prescribed by the supervising physician for asthma, COPD, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, congestive heart failure, HIV or AIDS, osteoporosis and co-morbidities identified by the supervising physician for the individual patient along with the primary diagnosis.
The agreement shall specifically reference each disease state being co-managed.
A retail patient shall be referred by a supervising physician to that physician's collaborating pharmacist, given notice of the collaboration, and consent to it.

247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)1.a. allows extension of current therapy by 30 days for not more than two 30 day periods, or as otherwise specifically authorized by the supervising physician in the referral and as provided in the agreement.

247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)1.b. allows initiating, modifying or discontinuing dosages of medications prescribed by the supervising physician for the eight named conditions and for co-morbidities listed among them and identified along with the primary diagnosis in the referral.

The regulatory prescribing authority requires a current Department registration to prescribe and possess controlled substances and an agreement with individually developed prescriptive practice guidelines under which the supervising physician has authorized the pharmacist to prescribe.
M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B3/4 provides that the regulations shall govern each agreement and shall be defined and limited by section 24B1/2 and chapter 94C.
No retail agreement may permit prescribing of Schedule II through V controlled substances, and no community pharmacist may prescribe or be authorized to prescribe them.

A retail pharmacist may issue Schedule VI prescriptions only under an agreement that specifically allows initial prescriptions for referred patients, for a diagnosis specified in the individual referral, with a copy sent to the supervising physician within 24 hours.

The community pharmacy agreement must provide that the supervising physician will give a written referral specifying the primary and any secondary diagnoses, copy it to the authorized pharmacist, and obtain the patient's written informed consent with a copy to the patient; 247 CMR 16.04(1) makes the written referral and written consent part of the agreement.

The authorized pharmacist and supervising physician each maintain a written record of the referral and consent; the physician keeps the original consent, transmits a copy of it to the pharmacist within 24 hours, and gives the patient copies of the referral and consent in a timely manner.
243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)4. requires the consent form to state that the pharmacist shall not replace the physician as the principal medical decision maker.

A retail drug business practicing collaborative drug therapy management shall not be required to register as a Health Facility under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(2)(d); in the current regulation Health Facility registration appears at 105 CMR 700.004(A)(3)(d).
247 CMR 16.03(5)(b) and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)2. provide that pharmacists, as authorized pursuant to a collaborative practice agreement, may administer vaccines.

decision_logic.condition: Is the practice taking place in a retail drug business under a current collaborative practice agreement?
decision_logic.action: If so, apply clause (5) of M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c) and 247 CMR 16.03(5); the hospital, long-term care, hospice and ambulatory care limbs are taught in the foundations section.

decision_logic.condition: Does the file hold the written referral specifying the primary and any secondary diagnoses, and the patient's written informed consent on a form carrying the statement 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)4. requires?
decision_logic.action: If not, the community pharmacy formalities are incomplete: the agreement must provide that the supervising physician supplies them, and 247 CMR 16.04(1) makes both documents part of the agreement.
Stop: the retail agreement cannot reach the patient, whatever the service requested, including a vaccine.

decision_logic.condition: Was the patient referred by the supervising physician to that physician's collaborating pharmacist, given notice of the collaboration, and did the patient consent?
decision_logic.action: If any element is missing, the patient is not yet within the retail collaboration.

decision_logic.condition: Does the request concern a disease state?
decision_logic.action: Confirm the condition is among the eight named conditions and that the agreement specifically references it; for a co-morbidity, confirm it is among the eight and was identified by the supervising physician along with the primary diagnosis in the referral.

decision_logic.condition: Is the request to extend current therapy?
decision_logic.action: Confirm the therapy is current and was prescribed by the supervising physician, that the pharmacist is currently registered by the Department to prescribe and possess controlled substances (247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)1.; 105 CMR 700.003(G)(2)), and that the agreement includes individually developed prescriptive practice guidelines under which the supervising physician has authorized the pharmacist to prescribe. With those in place, one extension of 30 days is within both the statute and the regulations, and anything further rests on the regulations' wording, read subject to M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B3/4.

decision_logic.condition: Does the request involve a Schedule II, III, IV or V controlled substance?
decision_logic.action: Decline under the agreement: neither an agreement term nor physician authorization can reach it.

decision_logic.condition: Is the request for a new Schedule VI prescription?
decision_logic.action: Confirm the agreement specifically allows initial prescriptions for referred patients and that the diagnosis is specified in the individual referral; if issued, a copy goes to the supervising physician within 24 hours.

decision_logic.condition: Is the request to administer a vaccine?
decision_logic.action: Confirm the agreement authorizes vaccine administration and that the patient is a referred, notified and consenting patient 18 or older. To meet the narrowest reading of clause (5) as well as the regulations, also confirm that the agreement specifically references the disease state and that the supervising physician prescribed the vaccine for that named condition or for a co-morbidity the physician identified along with the primary diagnosis. A vaccine given without that prescription, or unrelated to those conditions, rests on 247 CMR 16.03(5)(b) and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)2., which require only authorization under the agreement, and on the reading that the statute's list does not reach vaccines, which the statute may not support under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B3/4. Authority outside an agreement is taught in the pharmacist administration section.

exceptions.text: The regulations' two-period limit on extending current therapy yields where a longer extension is otherwise specifically authorized by the supervising physician in the referral of the patient and as provided in the agreement.

Schedule VI is the one controlled substance category a retail collaborating pharmacist may prescribe, and only under the statutory conditions on initial prescriptions, the referral diagnosis and the 24-hour copy.

timing_deadlines.event: Extension of current drug therapy prescribed by the supervising physician
timing_deadlines.timeframe: By 30 days under the statute; by 30 days for not more than two 30 day periods, or as otherwise specifically authorized in the referral and agreement, under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)1.a.
timing_deadlines.consequence: An extension beyond one 30-day period rests on the regulations' wording rather than the statute's; a single 30-day extension is within both.

timing_deadlines.event: Patient's written consent obtained in the community pharmacy setting
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Supervising physician transmits a copy of the consent to the authorized pharmacist within 24 hours; copies of the referral and consent go to the patient in a timely manner
timing_deadlines.consequence: A consent copy reaching the pharmacist after 24 hours does not meet 247 CMR 16.03(5)(d)2. or 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)5.

timing_deadlines.event: Schedule VI prescription issued by a retail collaborating pharmacist
timing_deadlines.timeframe: A copy of the prescription sent to the supervising physician within 24 hours
timing_deadlines.consequence: A copy sent after 24 hours does not meet the statutory requirement.

forms_records.text: The collaborative practice agreement for the retail setting specifically references each disease state being co-managed.

For Schedule VI prescribing, the agreement specifically allows initial prescriptions for referred patients of the supervising physician, and the supervising physician's individual referral of the patient specifies the diagnosis for which the prescription is issued.

For the regulatory prescribing authority, the agreement includes individually developed prescriptive practice guidelines under which the supervising physician has authorized the pharmacist to prescribe, and the pharmacist holds a current Department registration to prescribe and possess controlled substances.
Any longer extension than two 30-day periods under the regulations is specifically authorized by the supervising physician in the referral of the patient and provided for in the agreement.
Co-morbidities to be managed under the regulations are identified by the supervising physician along with the primary diagnosis in the referral.
A copy of each Schedule VI prescription issued under clause (5) is sent to the supervising physician within 24 hours.

In the community pharmacy setting the CDTM agreement includes a written referral of a specific patient from the supervising physician to the authorized pharmacist and the written consent of the patient to the agreement.
The written referral specifies the primary diagnosis and any secondary diagnoses, which may instead be specified in a subsequent referral.
The patient's written consent form includes the statement "The pharmacist shall not replace the physician as the principal medical decision maker." under 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)4.

A written record of the individual patient referral and of the patient's written informed consent is kept in the patient's records maintained by the authorized pharmacist and by the supervising physician; the original consent stays in the record in the supervising physician's custody.

Vaccine administration under a community pharmacy agreement requires the agreement's authorization, so the agreement is the document that shows it; for the course that meets the narrowest reading of clause (5), the supervising physician's prescription of the vaccine for a named condition or identified co-morbidity the agreement references is the further document that shows it.

role_duties.duty: Supervise the retail collaborating pharmacist according to the terms of the agreement; refer each patient to that physician's own collaborating pharmacist; specify in the individual referral the diagnosis for any Schedule VI prescription and identify any co-morbidity along with the primary diagnosis; and, as a party to the agreement, settle in it whether initial prescriptions are specifically allowed and whether vaccine administration is authorized.

role_duties.role: Collaborating pharmacist in a retail drug business
role_duties.duty: Act only for referred, notified and consenting patients 18 or older, for disease states the agreement specifically references; extend only current therapy the supervising physician prescribed; prescribe no Schedule II through V substance; issue Schedule VI prescriptions only under the statutory conditions; and administer vaccines only as the agreement authorizes.

role_duties.role: Supervising physician in the community pharmacy setting (referral and consent)
role_duties.duty: Provide the written referral and a copy of it to the authorized pharmacist, specifying the primary and any secondary diagnoses; obtain the patient's written informed consent and give the patient a copy; keep the original consent in the record in his custody; transmit a copy of the consent to the pharmacist within 24 hours; and provide copies of the referral and consent to the patient in a timely manner.

role_duties.role: Authorized pharmacist in the community pharmacy setting (records)
role_duties.duty: Maintain a written record of the individual patient referral and of the patient's written informed consent to the collaboration in the patient's records the pharmacist maintains.

role_duties.role: Retail drug business practicing collaborative drug therapy management
role_duties.duty: Not required to register as a Health Facility under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(2)(d) (the statute's cross-reference; the current regulation places Health Facility registration at 105 CMR 700.004(A)(3)(d)) because it practices collaborative drug therapy management under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(d).

role_duties.role: Pharmacist relying on the regulatory prescribing authority
role_duties.duty: Hold a current Department registration to prescribe and possess controlled substances and practise under an agreement with individually developed prescriptive practice guidelines under which the supervising physician has authorized prescribing.

common_traps.text: Treating a condition on the statutory list as automatically co-managed for a patient. The agreement shall specifically reference each disease state being co-managed.

Answering an extension question on the statute alone or on the regulations alone. The statute speaks of an extension by 30 days; the regulations allow not more than two 30 day periods or a longer specifically authorized extension.
Extending therapy the supervising physician did not prescribe, or therapy that is not current.
Carrying the statute's co-morbidity words into the regulations. 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)1.b. reaches only co-morbidities listed among the eight conditions.
Reading the Schedule II through V bar as ending at Schedule IV, or as something a physician's written approval can overcome.
Treating authority to modify or extend therapy as authority to issue an initial Schedule VI prescription. The agreement must specifically allow initial prescriptions for referred patients.
Writing a Schedule VI prescription for a diagnosis the pharmacist identifies rather than one specified in the supervising physician's individual referral.

Placing the community pharmacy referral and consent duties on the pharmacist. 247 CMR 16.03(5)(c) requires the agreement to provide that the supervising physician will supply the referral and obtain the consent.
Checking a consent form against 247 CMR 16.03(5) alone and missing the statement 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)4. requires: the pharmacist shall not replace the physician as the principal medical decision maker.
Attaching the 24 hours to the copies owed to the patient. The 24 hours govern the physician's transmission of the consent copy to the pharmacist; the patient's copies are due in a timely manner.
Reading M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(d) as relieving the pharmacist of the Department registration for prescribing. It speaks to the retail drug business and Health Facility registration.
Reading the vaccine item in 247 CMR 16.03(5)(b) as free of the setting's other requirements. The age floor and the referral, notice and consent requirements still apply.

Presenting M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B3/4 as settling every difference of wording. It says the regulations shall be defined and limited by section 24B1/2, and does not itself say how a differently worded regulation is to be read.

drug_examples.teaching_point: Pregabalin is in Schedule V, which is inside the Schedule II through V range that no retail agreement may permit a pharmacist to prescribe, even for a co-morbidity of a listed condition.

Insulin glargine is a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug used in diabetes, a listed condition: a retail pharmacist may modify dosages the supervising physician prescribed where the agreement references diabetes, and may issue an initial prescription only where the agreement specifically allows initial prescriptions and the referral specifies the diagnosis.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: In the retail drug business setting collaborative practice is limited to PATIENTS 18 YEARS OF AGE OR OLDER; to AN EXTENSION BY 30 DAYS of current drug therapy prescribed by the supervising physician; and to administration of vaccines or the modification of dosages of medications prescribed by the supervising physician for the named disease states and co-morbidities identified by the supervising physician for the individual patient along with the primary diagnosis.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws
Acts of 2008, Chapter 528 (An Act establishing collaborative drug therapy management)

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c)(5) allows collaborative drug therapy management by a collaborating pharmacist in a retail drug business, as registered in section 38 of chapter 112 and limited by this section, with supervision by a physician according to the terms of his collaborative practice agreement and limited to the following: patients 18 years of age or older; an extension by 30 days of current drug therapy prescribed by the supervising physician; and administration of vaccines or the modification of dosages of medications prescribed by the supervising physician for asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, congestive heart failure, HIV or AIDS, osteoporosis and co-morbidities identified by the supervising physician for the individual patient along with the primary diagnosis. The collaborative practice agreement shall specifically reference each disease state being co-managed. A patient shall be referred by a supervising physician to that physician's collaborating pharmacist and shall be given notice of the collaboration and shall consent to the collaboration. The clause was inserted by St. 2008, c. 528, s. 3, approved January 15, 2009, and the current text of clause (5) reads as enacted.

authority.name: Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations
Board of Registration in Medicine regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: 247 CMR 16.03 provides that, in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c), collaborative drug therapy management may be performed in the listed settings by pharmacists meeting the requirements of 247 CMR 16.02(1) and authorized by a supervising physician pursuant to a current collaborative practice agreement. 247 CMR 16.03(5) lists Community Pharmacies (retail drug business settings) licensed by the Board pursuant to M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39, subject to the restrictions listed below it and pursuant to a current collaborative practice agreement that includes the following requirements: (a) Patient Age, patients must be 18 years of age or older; (b) Vaccine Administration, pharmacists, as authorized pursuant to a collaborative practice agreement, may administer vaccines; (c) Patient Referral and Consent; (d) Record of Referral and Consent; and (e) Limited Prescribing Authority. 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)1. and 2. state the same age and vaccine items for the Board of Registration in Medicine.

authority.name: Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations
Board of Registration in Medicine regulations
authority.section: 243 CMR 2.12(1), definition of CDTM agreement; 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)3., 4. and 5.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(c), in accordance with 243 CMR 2.12, the collaborative practice agreement for a community pharmacy must provide that the supervising physician will: 1. provide a written referral of the patient to the authorized pharmacist; 2. specify the primary diagnosis for the patient and any secondary diagnoses in the written referral or a subsequent referral; 3. provide a copy of the written referral of the patient to the authorized pharmacist for CDTM services to the patient; and 4. obtain the patient's written informed consent to the collaboration in the collaborative practice agreement and provide a copy of the consent to the patient. Under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(d), the authorized pharmacist and supervising physician must maintain a written record of both the individual patient referral and the patient's written informed consent to the collaboration in the patient's records which are maintained by the authorized pharmacist and the supervising physician; and, in accordance with 243 CMR 2.12, the supervising physician shall maintain the original patient consent to the referral in the record in the custody of the supervising physician, transmit a copy of the patient's consent to the authorized pharmacist within 24 hours, and provide copies of the referral and consent to the patient in a timely manner. Under 247 CMR 16.04(1), in the community pharmacy setting the CDTM agreement shall include (a) a written referral of a specific patient from the supervising physician to an authorized pharmacist and (b) the written consent of the patient to the CDTM agreement. 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)3. and 5. state the referral, consent and record items in substantially the same words, 243 CMR 2.12(1) states that in the community pharmacy setting the CDTM agreement shall include a written referral of an identified patient and a written consent to the CDTM agreement by the named patient, and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)4. adds that the patient's written consent form shall include the statement: "The pharmacist shall not replace the physician as the principal medical decision maker."

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(d), a retail drug business practicing in collaborative drug therapy management under this section shall not be required to register as a Health Facility under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(2)(d).

authority.name: Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations
Board of Registration in Medicine regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)1., an authorized pharmacist currently registered by the Department, pursuant to M.G.L. c. 94C, ss. 7 and 9 and 105 CMR 700.000, to prescribe and possess controlled substances, who practices in a community pharmacy pursuant to a collaborative practice agreement that includes individually developed prescriptive practice guidelines pursuant to which the supervising physician has authorized the pharmacist to prescribe, may: a. extend current drug therapy by 30 days for not more than two 30 day periods or as may otherwise be specifically authorized by the supervising physician in the referral of the patient and as provided in the CDTM agreement; and b. initiate, modify or discontinue dosages of medications prescribed by the supervising physician for asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, congestive heart failure, HIV or AIDS, osteoporosis, and co-morbidities listed in i. through viii. and identified by the supervising physician along with the primary diagnosis in the supervising physician's referral of the patient. 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)6.a. and b. state the same authority.
exceptions: The two-period limit on extensions yields where a longer extension is otherwise specifically authorized by the supervising physician in the referral of the patient and as provided in the CDTM agreement.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B3/4 requires the board of registration in medicine and the board of registration in pharmacy to issue rules and regulations to implement collaborative drug therapy management pursuant to section 24B1/2 and sections 7 and 9 of chapter 94C, and provides that the rules and regulations shall govern each collaborative practice agreement and shall be defined and limited by section 24B1/2, chapter 94C and other applicable statutes. Among the issues the boards shall address is the scope of conditions or diseases to be managed, the initial list of which shall not include more than 5 disease states, the 5 diseases selected for the retail setting to be from among those referenced in clause (5) of subsection (c) of section 24B1/2. The boards shall reconsider the regulations on a periodic basis, as considered appropriate by the commissioner, for the purposes of adding or removing disease states and of updating the rules and regulations as necessary.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c)(5), a pharmacist in the retail setting who has a collaborative practice agreement with a supervising physician which specifically allows initial prescriptions for referred patients of the supervising physician may issue prescriptions for schedule VI controlled substances, as defined in clause 6 of section 3 of chapter 94C. Such prescriptions shall be for a patient diagnosis specified in the supervising physician's individual referral of that patient. A copy of the prescription shall be sent to the supervising physician within 24 hours.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c)(5), no collaborative practice agreement in the retail drug business setting may permit the prescribing of schedule II through V controlled substances, as defined in section 3 of chapter 94C.

authority.name: Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations
Board of Registration in Medicine regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)3., no authorized pharmacist in a community pharmacy may prescribe or be authorized to prescribe Schedule II through V controlled substances, as defined in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 3, subsections (2) through (5). Under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)4., an authorized pharmacist in a community pharmacy may be authorized by a supervising physician to issue prescriptions for Schedule VI controlled substances, as defined in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 3, subsection (6), for the diagnoses specified in the supervising physician's patient referral. 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)7. and 8. state the same bar and authorization.

authority.name: Massachusetts Department of Public Health regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 105 CMR 700.003(G)(4) the pharmacist, IF PRACTICING IN A RETAIL SETTING, may issue a prescription for a controlled substance IN SCHEDULE VI ONLY, in accordance with 105 CMR 700.003(G)(3).
exceptions: The subparagraph is addressed to a pharmacist practising in a retail setting; it states no ceiling for a pharmacist practising elsewhere.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws
Massachusetts General Laws
Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations
Board of Registration in Medicine regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c)(5) limits retail collaborative practice to, among other things, administration of vaccines or the modification of dosages of medications prescribed by the supervising physician for asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, congestive heart failure, HIV or AIDS, osteoporosis and co-morbidities identified by the supervising physician for the individual patient along with the primary diagnosis. The statute's words do not state separately whether the list of conditions reaches the vaccine limb; if it does, it reaches it only through the words prescribed by the supervising physician for, so on that reading the vaccine is one the supervising physician prescribed for a named condition or identified co-morbidity. 247 CMR 16.03(5)(b) and 243 CMR 2.12(4)(e)2. state vaccine administration as a separate item: pharmacists, as authorized pursuant to a collaborative practice agreement, may administer vaccines, with no disease list and no requirement of a supervising-physician prescription. Under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B3/4 the rules and regulations shall govern each collaborative practice agreement and shall be defined and limited by section 24B1/2, chapter 94C and other applicable statutes.

authority.name: Massachusetts Department of Public Health regulations
Massachusetts General Laws

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: In the current 105 CMR 700.004(A), paragraph (2) lists the practitioners required to be registered under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1), with (2)(d) Nurse Midwife and (2)(f) Pharmacist, and paragraph (3) lists the facilities that shall register for the purpose of purchase and storage of controlled substances in Massachusetts, with (3)(d) Health Facility. M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(d) states its Health Facility cross-reference as 105 CMR 700.004(A)(2)(d); in the current regulation Health Facility registration appears at 105 CMR 700.004(A)(3)(d).

authority.name: Massachusetts Department of Public Health regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: The pharmacist registers with the Department, in accordance with 105 CMR 700.004, and with the DEA IF APPLICABLE in accordance with 21 CFR 1300, FOR THE PURPOSE OF PRESCRIBING under 105 CMR 700.000. The purpose of the registration is part of the requirement, so a registration obtained for dispensing does not carry prescribing authority, and the federal limb bites only where it is applicable.
exceptions: The DEA limb applies only if applicable
